title: Obama Calls Midterms a 'Circuit Breaker' on Trump in Detroit and Cleveland
excerpt: Ten days before the November 3 vote, the former president accused Trump of corruption, attacked his Iran and tariff policies, and stumped for Senate candidates Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan and Sherrod Brown in Ohio.
body:
• Former President Barack Obama campaigned in Cleveland and Detroit on Saturday, October 24, ten days before the November 3 midterms, framing the vote as a "circuit breaker" to rein in President Donald Trump's administration.
  • In Detroit, Obama headlined a rally of more than 4,000 people at Cass Technical High School for Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed, who faces Republican former Rep. Mike Rogers for an open seat rated a toss-up.
  • For readers: Michigan's midterm ballot is decided November 3, early in-person voting is now underway in the state, and control of the closely divided U.S. Senate runs through races in Michigan and Ohio.
  • Obama accused Trump of corruption and profiting from office, attacked his Iran strategy and Canada tariffs, and mocked the gold-heavy White House renovations; the White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Former President Barack Obama took to the campaign trail on Saturday with rallies in Cleveland and Detroit, telling voters ten days before the midterm elections that the November 3 vote is their chance to put a check on President Donald Trump. Campaigning in Michigan for U.S. Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed, Obama framed the election as a "circuit breaker" to "at least rein in some of the foolishness" of Trump's presidency, according to Reuters.

"We got to flip that circuit breaker, bring some accountability to this government," Obama said. In Detroit, the Detroit Free Press reported, he put it as the country's "last, best chance" to rein in the administration, in a nearly 40-minute speech at Cass Technical High School before a crowd of more than 4,000 that spilled into an overflow space.

A direct attack on Trump

Obama accused the Republican president of corruption, derided his strategy on Iran and skewered the gilded aesthetic he has applied to White House renovations. "We have never seen a president excel in straight-up grifting, on your dime, like this," he said. "Never seen a president so intent on selling favors like this." A Reuters/Ipsos poll in August found 63% of Americans believe Trump and his family have inappropriately profited from cryptocurrency since he returned to the White House, and 69% believe his policy decisions are influenced by his private business dealings.

On Iran, Obama argued the war has handed Tehran leverage, saying Iran now has "veto power over the Strait of Hormuz, where oil goes through to get to the world." He ridiculed the focus on White House renovations — "He's got the White House looking like Saddam Hussein opened a Cheesecake Factory" — and, in Detroit, mocked tariffs on Canada, Detroit's neighbor across the river. The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment, Reuters reported. Earlier Saturday, Trump had called Obama a "lousy president" and was set to rally for Republican candidates in Port Huron, Michigan, on Sunday.

Why Michigan and Ohio matter

The two-state swing targeted the Senate races that could decide control of the closely divided chamber. In Michigan, El-Sayed, a former Wayne County and Detroit health director, faces Republican Mike Rogers, a former U.S. representative backed by Trump who narrowly lost a Senate race in 2024. Analysts rate the open-seat race a toss-up; a mid-October Marist survey put El-Sayed ahead within the margin of error. In Cleveland, Obama appeared with former Sen. Sherrod Brown, who is challenging Republican Sen. Jon Husted for the seat once held by Vice President JD Vance, and with Democratic gubernatorial nominee Amy Acton.

Obama also defended El-Sayed against attacks on his background — El-Sayed would be the first Muslim and first Egyptian American in the U.S. Senate if he wins. "We have seen this movie before. I starred in it. I've got a long form birth certificate to prove it," Obama said. "This stuff didn't work on me, not in Michigan. It's not going to work on Abdul." He urged Democrats to offer an affirmative agenda: "We can't just be against something, we gotta be for something."

What it means for the diaspora

For Indian American voters, the midterms will shape the congressional balance that decides immigration, H-1B and trade policy for the next two years — the same Michigan and Ohio Senate races Obama targeted are among the handful that will determine which party controls that agenda. Michigan's early in-person voting began the day of the Detroit rally, and voters there can already cast ballots ahead of November 3.

What comes next

Obama's outreach is expanding in the closing stretch, with additional stops and advertisements expected, including a Georgia rally next week. In Michigan, Sen. Bernie Sanders was set to campaign with El-Sayed in Grand Rapids on Sunday as Trump stumped for Rogers nearby — a final-ten-days collision that underlines how much both parties are investing in a state Obama carried in 2008 and 2012 and that now sits at the center of the fight for the Senate.
